records.name: Kosovo
records.summary_text: Kosovo is workable for trans visitors — the Balkans' strongest legal framework on paper. The constitution (Art 24) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination covers gender identity; legal gender recognition is possible (medicalised); and the government attempted same-sex unions in 2024 as part of Council of Europe accession. Counterweights: implementation is inconsistent, political hate speech is common (2022 CSGD report: year marked by intolerance), and Pristina Pride proceeds under protection.

records.name: Gibraltar
records.summary_text:
Gibraltar legislates its own civil and criminal law as a self-governing territory on the Iberian peninsula's southern tip. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1993 with an equal age of consent since 2012; discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment date from 2007; civil partnerships followed in 2014, and same-sex marriage was enacted unanimously in December 2016 after a 2015 public consultation returned overwhelming support (3,490 replies from a 24,117-person electorate).

records.name: Bermuda
records.summary_text:
Bermuda decriminalised private adult same-sex conduct in 1994 (House of Assembly, 22-16) and in 2013 outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Same-sex marriages performed in 2017 were withdrawn the following year by a Domestic Partnership Act — the first jurisdiction anywhere to reverse marriage equality — and in March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld that restoration of the traditional-marriage definition, so partnerships, not marriage, are the available status for same-sex couples.

records.name: Anguilla
records.summary_text:
Anguilla's prohibitions were removed around 2000-2001 — a recent first-person travel account puts the change at 2000, the contemporaneous wire coverage of the Caribbean-wide reform at January 2001 — again by imposition from London after local reluctance. Same-sex relationships are simply not an issue in the public sense because there is almost no public LGBT life: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers and same-sex wedding tourism pitched on 'friendly, relaxed atmosphere.'
